title: A performance refactor of AdminPermission.projects split one combined Q filter into chained .filter(teams__members=user).filter(teams__access=ADMIN_ACCESS) calls, so read-only team members get admin rights on any project that also belongs to some admin team.

findings.explanation: The change only restructures ORM queryset filtering using Django's Q objects and chained .filter() calls. No raw SQL, string interpolation, or user-controlled input is passed directly to a query.

The original code used a single .filter(filter, teams__members=user) call that combined both the access-level condition and the team membership check atomically in one JOIN. The refactored code first filters by teams__members=user and then, in a separate .filter() call, filters by teams__access. When chaining multiple .filter() calls in Django ORM for ManyToMany relations, each .filter() generates a separate JOIN, which can cause cross-join artifacts: a project could be returned if the user is a member of one team and another team (of that project) has the required access level — not necessarily the same team. This could allow a read-only team member to pass an admin access check. The new 'else' branch (both admin and member True) is safe, but the admin-only and member-only branches may have incorrect authorization semantics.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the original single .filter() call that combines both conditions in one queryset to avoid Django ORM multi-JOIN cross-matching: use filter(Q(teams__members=user) & Q(teams__access=...)) or revert to the original pattern using a combined Q expression passed as a single filter call, ensuring that the membership and access checks apply to the same team row.
